blocks.title: Intensity
blocks.text: Intensity is defined as the amount of energy transmitted per unit area per unit time in the direction of propagation of a progressive wave. It is a measure of the power of a wave, is usually denoted by the symbol I, and is measured in watts per square metre (W m^-2).

A progressive or travelling wave is one that travels through a medium in a consistent direction and transfers energy from one point to another; it propagates or moves forward, as opposed to a stationary or standing wave. Examples of progressive waves include water waves, sound waves and light waves. By definition the intensity of a wave is I = E/(A x t) = (E/t)/A, or I = P/A (since E/t = P), where I is the intensity in W m^-2, E the energy in joules, t the time in seconds, A the area and P the power in watts.

In mechanical waves, such as sound waves, water waves or waves on a vibrating string, energy is stored as kinetic energy and potential energy of the medium's particles. How much energy is stored depends upon the displacement (amplitude) of the particles from the mean position; therefore the intensity I of waves is proportional to the square of the amplitude A: I is proportional to A^2, or I = k A^2 ... (7.13). Here k is the constant of proportionality and depends upon the physical properties of the wave and the medium. Frequency and amplitude of a travelling wave are independent of each other; that is why you can turn up the volume of a song (increase the amplitude) without changing its pitch, which depends on frequency (Tidbits). Sound cannot travel through vacuum, as there are no particles to transmit the sound wave (Tidbits).

blocks.title: Example 7.8
blocks.text: (a) A wave has an intensity of 0.5 W m^-2 at a distance of 3.0 m from the source. What is the power of the wave? (b) Two progressive waves have intensities of 0.5 W m^-2 and 0.25 W m^-2; find the total intensity. Solution: (a) I = 0.5 W m^-2, r = 3.0 m, P = ?. As I = P/A = P/(4 pi r^2), 0.5 = P/(4 x 3.14 x (3.0)^2), so P = 0.5 x 113.04 = 56.52 W (printed as 'P = 0.51 x 13.04'). (b) I1 = 0.5 W m^-2, I2 = 0.25 W m^-2, I = I1 + I2 = 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75 W m^-2.

blocks.title: Example 7.9
blocks.text: A speaker emits sound waves with a power of 50 W. If the sound waves spread out evenly in all directions and the intensity is measured at a distance of 5 m from the speaker, what is the intensity if the area of the sphere at that distance is approximately 314 m^2? Solution: P = 50 W, A = 314 m^2; intensity = power/area, I = P/A = 50 W / 314 m^2, about 0.159 W m^-2.

blocks.prompt: If the amplitude of a wave is tripled, by how much is its energy increased (MCQ 7.8)? If I = 16 W m^-2 when A = 2 m, find k; if I = 25 W m^-2 and k = 5 W m^-4, find A. A 500 W radio antenna: what is the intensity 10 km away (numerical 7.6, 7.8)?
blocks.explanation: I is proportional to A^2, so tripling A multiplies the energy by 9. k = I/A^2 = 16/4 = 4 W m^-4; A = sqrt(I/k) = sqrt(25/5) = 2.24 m. I = P/(4 pi r^2) = 500/(4 x 3.14 x (10^4)^2) = 500/1.26 x 10^9 = 4 x 10^-7 W m^-2.

items: Intensity: energy per unit area per unit time in the direction of a progressive wave, W m^-2: I = E/(A t) = P/A; for a point source A = 4 pi r^2. I = k A^2 (7.13): energy grows as the square of the amplitude; amplitude (volume) and frequency (pitch) are independent. Examples: 56.52 W; 0.75 W m^-2; 0.159 W m^-2.
